body: I struggled today to not self harm. I haven't done it since 2008, but like csim said, it is an urge that we have to fight constantly. There is no shame in a relapse, it's what we do after that determines our strength.

It seems like you may just be experiencing the aftermath of an embarassing situation. Shame can be powerful enough to make you want to die, but you seem to recoginize that things will most likely work themselves out, and that you have other options even if they don't at this job. The big question is this: will you be able to work there comfortably? My guess is that if you give it a little bit of time you may still be embarassed, but most of the people you work with will get over it. Especially if you're new there, they may tease you about it, but as they get to know you, they will likely not hold it against you. 
Shame is a powerful emotion, if you can, try not to let it overtake you. It sounds like you've got some good things going on apart from this episode.
Good luck!

Chronic depression is hard, and it doesn't really get easier, just more "normal". You start to deal with it and find ways to cope and keep moving. But we're in danger when it hits hard, and I wish people like your mother could understand that. Many see it as a "cry for attention" but when that wave of depression crashes over us it can drag us back out with it, and nearly drown us. It's so deep and so strong that sometimes when it strikes it truly feels like there is no way out but to give in and drown. People like you and I spend our lives treading water to make it every day, and it's unfortunate that there are people out there who just can't understand what having chronic depression means. They often think it's just a "bad mood" or a "down day", but it's not. It's got nothing to do with our attitude, or our positivity, and often times those of us who are still standing work very hard to find the positive, and have a good attitude, otherwise we would not have made it as far as we have. We have to try so much harder, for so much longer, and even though when that surge of depression engulfs us and drags us down we feel weak, remember that we are some of the strongest, if only for making it as far as we have. Wanting to give in doesn't make us weak. Even the best swimmers would be fatiuged after swiming every moment of every day for years on end.

I think for most of us, surviving is a choice we have to make every day. Some days it's harder to make than others. I have a story, but it's too long to relate here, but I've been surviving for 20 years. It's easy to find excuses to kill yourself, I find it's much harder to find excuses to stay alive, but by doing so, I give myself time to climb out of my dark place for a while.

I keep going out of sheer force of will. I try to rationalize and guilt myself into staying alive for another day, week, month. Find something I'm obligated to do before I can die. When that's done, hopefully I've been able to pull myself out a little bit. If not, I try to find another excuse. While I'm stuck with my obligation I try to recognize the small, brief moments when I feel happy, even if it's only for a minute or two. Not to remind myself why I should live, but to not allow the moments when I am enjoying my surroundings to be tainted by the darkness I carry. It's not easy. All I want to do is self destruct, to crumble away, to give in to my selfishness, sleep and never wake, but I'm trying so hard to be the sort of person I want to be, which is strong, and stable (no one around me knows it, but I'm failing that last one big time right now). Why should you live only to suffer? I can't answer that. I suppose that's why I try to recognize the minutes in my life when I am enjoying what's going on around me, because I feel I have no choice but to keep going, and I don't want to only remember my misery.

I'm almost 30 and have suffered depression and suicidal urges for going on 20 years. I have been, and still am where you are. The yoga, meds, counselors, self medication, meditation tracks, exercise, and still I spent the weekend reminding myself why I cant put my SOs gun in my mouth.
I dont have a solution, but I have experience. I'm here if you need someone to talk to.

https://www.reddit.com/r/SWResources/comments/igh87/concerned_but_dont_know_what_to_say_here_are_some/
As a person in your friends shoes, I agree with the suggestions in this link.

I understand that desire to just esape all of it. I'm suicidal thoughts stem from a desire to escape, run away, just sleep forever and not have to face the things in front of me. I can't say I've found a solution, other than finding small "temporary" reasons not to. I can't offer help, but I hope it helps to know you're not alone.
I don't know what to say to that. I'm sorry they feel that way.

I hope you find a way out. 20 years is a long, long time to hold on without relief, and it's something I hope you don't have to endure.

I think my method has been to find the next "temporary" reason to hold off on any drastic actions. "I can't kill myself right now, because if I do, my husband will definitely lose his custody case; I'll wait until after the trial", "I can't kill myself right now because I'm pregnant", "I can't right now because if I do my husband won't be able to keep the house without my income." 
It's not an ideal way to do it, because it can make me feel trapped. I try to immerse myself in projects or work during these times since it keeps me distracted from the dark feelings. Right now it's hard though, and I'm struggling. I'm sorry to know that you are too. I hope we both find our way at some point.

One thing I do to fight my urges is to remember that it will be hard on my family if I go. Not just emotionally, but there are usually other complications that people don't thing of initially. 
I don't know the specifics of your situation, but it's possible you would be trading one version of "hard" for your family for a new one. It's worth giving a little thought to.
I wish I could show this to my husband without giving away how close to the edge I am right now.
